summary: KS3 (age 11-13) learners extend accurate ruler-and-protractor work in two directions: constructing a triangle from a specification (e.g. two sides and the included angle, SAS) to the nearest degree and millimetre, and interpreting scale drawings to extract real measurements. Construction carries forward the protractor hazards of earlier years — reading the wrong scale on a dual-scale protractor (drawing the supplement) and misplacing vertex/baseline — now under a tighter accuracy demand. Scale drawing introduces a well-documented conceptual hazard: reasoning ADDITIVELY about scale (adding a constant) instead of MULTIPLICATIVELY (multiplying by a scale factor), and dropping or muddling units when converting. Effective teaching keeps the estimate-first placement routine for construction, and for scale makes the multiplicative structure explicit — 'each 1 cm on the drawing stands for so many metres, so I multiply' — with pictorial models, precise language about dimensions, and reasonableness checks.
misconceptions: Reasons additively about scale — adds a constant difference rather than multiplying by the scale factor — the classic additive-strategy error, most common in the ratio/proportion literature
Drops or muddles units in a scale conversion, or treats 'size' loosely (confusing length scale with area scale)
Reads the wrong scale on the dual-scale protractor, measuring/drawing the supplement of the intended angle
Misplaces the protractor centre or zero-line, so measured angles are consistently a few degrees out
Accepts a nearly-closing constructed triangle as accurate rather than as evidence of accumulated placement/measurement error

activities.title: SAS construction with the estimate-first protractor routine
steps: Construct a triangle from two sides of 6 cm and 8 cm with an included angle of 55° between them: rule the first side from the ruler's zero, place the protractor with its centre on the endpoint vertex and zero-line along the side, set the 55° angle, measure and mark the second side, then rule the third side to close the triangle

Before reading the protractor, estimate first: 'Is 55° bigger or smaller than a right angle (a square corner)?' Smaller, so choose the scale that gives a value under 90°, not the 125° on the other scale

Because you finish by joining the two free endpoints, an SAS triangle always closes, so closing does not show it is accurate. Instead, measure the third side and the other two angles and compare them with the expected values. For 6 cm, 8 cm and 55°, the third side should be about 6.7 cm and the other angles about 47° and 78°, and all three angles add up to 180°. A clear mismatch signals placement or measurement error: recheck the vertex placement, the zero-line and the scale you chose
Aim for accuracy to about the nearest degree and nearest millimetre
activities.insight: Accurate construction depends on a disciplined sequence (base → included angle → side → join the endpoints) and on choosing the right scale on a dual-scale protractor by first estimating against a right angle. Joining the endpoints always closes an SAS triangle, so accuracy is checked by comparing the measured third side (about 6.7 cm) and remaining angles (about 47° and 78°) with the expected values, not by whether the triangle closes.

activities.title: Scale conversion as a multiplier, not an addition
steps: On a printed or on-screen scale plan labelled 'Scale: 1 cm represents 2 m', measure a wall to the nearest millimetre (e.g. read 4.5 cm)

Convert to the real length by multiplying: write 'real = drawn × scale', so 4.5 cm × 2 m per cm = 9 m, carrying the units through the whole conversion. Equivalently, with the unitless scale factor of 1:200, 4.5 cm × 200 = 900 cm = 9 m
State the scale in words: 'each 1 cm on the drawing is 2 m in real life, so I multiply'
Use a double number line or ratio table linking drawn cm to real m to keep the multiplier visible
Check the real length is reasonable for the object (e.g. a 9 m wall in a room)

Explore what happens when the scale changes, as a thought experiment about the scale factor: imagine the same drawn length read at a different scale — if 1 cm represented 5 m (a 1:500 scale) instead of 2 m (a 1:200 scale), the real length multiplies, so the same 4.5 cm would stand for 22.5 m while the drawn length on the plan stays the same. Apply the reasonableness check to whatever object and scale are actually given — at 1:500 the plan would depict a correspondingly larger space
activities.insight: Scale is a multiplicative relationship: real length = drawn length × scale factor (and drawn = real ÷ factor). Changing the scale factor multiplies the real length while the drawing is unchanged; adding a constant does not model scale.

activities.title: Feeling the scale factor by zooming from plan to real room
steps: Starting from a floor-plan with a stated scale (e.g. 1 cm represents 2 m), zoom from the plan into a representation of the actual-size room to experience how a small drawn length corresponds to a large real one
Connect the visual expansion back to the number: a 4.5 cm wall on the plan becomes a 9 m wall in reality at 1 cm : 2 m
Return to the plan and do the measuring and conversion numerically
activities.insight: A scale factor can be made viscerally real by seeing a drawn length expand to its actual size, reinforcing that the real object is the drawing multiplied by the factor.

activities.title: Check scale reasoning and protractor scale choice (recognition practice)
steps: Answer a conversion item such as: a wall measures 4.5 cm on a plan at 1 cm : 2 m — what is the real length? Choose from options that include an additive distractor (6.5 m from adding) and a units-dropped distractor ('9' with no units) alongside the correct 9 m
Answer a 'which scale reads this angle?' item: given an angle estimated smaller than a right angle, decide which of the two protractor scales to read
Explain in words why you multiply rather than add, and why the units matter
activities.insight: Recognising additive and units-dropped distractors and choosing the correct protractor scale reinforces the multiplicative structure and the estimate-first habit; recognising the right answer among options is not the same as independently constructing or converting, so this consolidates rather than replaces the full task.

checkQuestion: Give the child a ruler, a protractor, and a printed scale drawing of a room or map labelled 'Scale: 1 cm represents 2 m'. Say: 'First, draw a triangle accurately with two sides of 6 cm and 8 cm and an angle of 55° between them. Then, on this plan, measure this wall and tell me its real length, and explain the scale you used.' Watch the construction and how they convert — do not talk them through it.
checkAnswer: Constructs the SAS triangle accurately (side ruled from the ruler's zero, 55° set with centre-on-vertex and the correct protractor scale, second side measured, third side ruled to close) to about ±2° / ±2 mm; measures the wall on the plan to the nearest millimetre and converts by multiplying by the scale factor (drawn length × 2 m per cm), keeping units, and explains 'each 1 cm on the drawing is 2 m in real life, so I multiply.'
